title: Looped Diffusion Transformer
relevance_reason: Weight-shared middle MMDiT blocks repeated N times inside each denoising step of a text-to-image diffusion model.
one_sentence: Loops 5 shared middle blocks of a 17-block pixel-space MMDiT 4 times per denoising step; deep supervision plus self-modulating attention (gated attention or XSA) make looping beat param-, inference-FLOP- and training-FLOP-matched baselines.
key_contributions: Shows naive looping in MMDiT saturates and degrades past training depth while linearly decodable spatial position collapses (probe R2 0.865 to 0.562).
Deep supervision of every loop through the shared post-loop stage plus self-modulating attention applied only inside the loop.
Controlled comparisons: loop depth beats extra denoising steps at matched inference FLOPs; gains persist vs deeper, wider, and deep-supervised deeper baselines; adaptive exit gate.

setup.model_sizes: Looped-DiT B/16 and B/32, 260M params (MiniT2I backbone, 17 blocks split 6/5/6, middle 5 looped)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: CC12M pretraining; fine-tune on BLIP3o-60K, DALL-E 3, ShareGPT-4o-Image; B/32 250K+40K steps, B/16 500K+80K steps
setup.baselines: MiniT2I B/32 param-matched; deeper (32 effective depth, 473M) and wider (1056 dim) inference-FLOP-matched; deeper with DeepSup training-FLOP-matched; public T2I models (InternVL-U, CogView4, SANA, CoT models)
setup.benchmarks: GenEval, DPG-Bench, PRISM, T2I-CoReBench, SpatialGenEval, TIIF-Short

claims.claim: Looped-DiT B/32 (260M) beats the param-matched non-looped MiniT2I B/32 by 4.0 avg points and also beats inference-FLOP-matched deeper/wider baselines that have more parameters; at matched training compute it scores 59.1 vs 58.1.
claims.regime: iso_param; iso_infer_flop; iso_train_flop; iso_effective_depth (deeper baseline has 32 effective depth); same training data
claims.evidence_quote: Looped-DiT B/32 improves the average score by 4.0 points over the parameter-matched baseline and outperforms both inference-compute-matched baselines despite using fewer parameters. Under matched training compute, it achieves 59.1 compared with 58.1 for the deeper baseline.

claims.claim: At matched per-image inference FLOPs, spending compute on loop depth beats spending it on more denoising steps.
claims.evidence_quote: From 25- to 50-step settings, allocating compute to loop depth consistently yields higher performance than allocating it to additional denoising steps, showing that looping is a more effective use of inference compute.

claims.claim: Naive looping fails: performance saturates and declines beyond training depth while spatial position information erodes; this motivates deep supervision and attention modulation.
claims.evidence_quote: As shown in Fig. 3(b), R2 drops from 0.865 after the 1st loop to 0.562 after 8th loops, an absolute decrease of 0.303, indicating that spatial position becomes progressively less linearly decodable.

claims.claim: Against public checkpoints, the 260M looped model beats a 6.5x larger model at 4.9x lower inference compute (different training data and recipes).
claims.evidence_quote: Notably, a 260M-parameter Looped-DiT outperforms non-looped models with roughly 6.5× more parameters across multiple text-to-image benchmarks while requiring 4.9× lower inference compute.

claims.claim: Looping and textual CoT prompt rewriting are complementary: looping helps constraint-resolution subtasks, CoT helps inferring implied content.
claims.regime: same checkpoint family; unclear compute matching
claims.evidence_quote: Consistent with the constraint-resolution and self-correction behavior observed above, Tab. 3 shows larger gains from looping on subtasks that require joint satisfaction of relational, procedural, or spatial constraints.

numbers.what: Table 2 avg score (B/32): param-matched MiniT2I B/32 vs Looped-DiT B/32
numbers.quote: Under matched training compute, it achieves 59.1 compared with 58.1 for the deeper baseline.

numbers.what: XSA gain for looped vs non-looped baselines
numbers.quote: Tab. 5 shows that XSA yields a larger gain for the looped model (+1.6) than for the parameter-matched (−0.1) and compute-matched (+0.7) non-looped baselines

numbers.what: Adaptive looping vs fixed-loop at matched mean loops
numbers.value: halves drop at 1.25 loops; plateau at 2.70 loops
numbers.quote: adaptive looping outperforms fixed-loop inference at matched mean loop counts, halves the performance drop in a few-loop setting (at 1.25 loops), and reaches a comparable performance plateau earlier (at 2.70 loops).

numbers.what: Gap to next-best public model InternVL-U
numbers.quote: Notably, compared with the next-best model, InternVL-U, Looped-DiT B/16 achieves a 2.5-point higher avg. score with 6.5× fewer parameters.

limitations: Only ~260M MiniT2I MMDiT at 512x512 pixel space; fixed [6,5,6] split and training depth 4; deep supervision raises training compute; latent-reasoning evidence is behavioral only.
survey_notes: Strongest controlled evidence in diffusion: one of few vision papers with iso-param, iso-inference-FLOP, iso-training-FLOP and iso-effective-depth baselines in one table (Table 2). Mirrors LM findings that naive looping saturates/degrades beyond training depth and that loop-wise supervision (cf. Ouro, TRM deep supervision) is needed. New: attention-update magnitude control (gated attention / XSA) only inside the loop; loop depth vs denoising steps as two test-time axes. Table 1 is unmatched (public checkpoints).

title: Procedural Core: A Compact Recurrent Initialization for Vision Transformers
relevance_reason: A weight-tied (recurrent-middle-block) auxiliary ViT is trained on procedural data; its weights are unrolled to initialize an untied target model, so looping is used only as a compression/regularization device for initialization.
one_sentence: Trains a ViT-Tiny with tied middle blocks (3 unique blocks, depth 12) on procedural data, then unrolls and tiles it to initialize untied ViTs and LMs of any size, beating random init (+2.2 pp ImageNet ViT-B).
key_contributions: Recurrent auxiliary model compresses procedural-data warm-up into ~1M reusable weights expanded in depth (unroll) and width (tile).
Ablation: recurrence matters; a parameter-matched non-recurrent 3-layer auxiliary transfers much less.
Mechanism: recurrence broadens singular spectrum; structure sits in attention value/output path and suppresses high-norm tokens.

setup.model_sizes: ~1M-parameter core; targets up to ViT-Base 85M; GPT-2-style LM targets
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Procedural data (formal languages) for core; ImageNet-1K, CIFAR-100, DINO, FineWeb-Edu, CodeParrot for targets
setup.loops_train: middle block tied across blocks 2..L-1 with L=12
setup.baselines: Random init, mimetic/structured init, direct procedural warm-up of target, parameter-matched non-recurrent auxiliary
setup.benchmarks: ImageNet-1K, CIFAR-100, ADE20K, ImageNet-S, VOC07 CorLoc, NYUv2, FineWeb-Edu, CodeParrot

claims.claim: A recurrent auxiliary model transfers far better than a parameter-matched non-recurrent auxiliary model (+4.7% vs +1.7% over random init on CIFAR-100 ViT-Tiny).
claims.evidence_quote: Moreover, a parameter-matched 3-layer non-recurrent model yields only a +1.7% improvement over the default random initialization, compared with +4.7% for our recurrent one (Figure 5b).

claims.claim: Expanding a 1M-parameter recurrent core to initialize ViT-Base improves ImageNet top-1 by 2.2 pp over random init.
claims.regime: same target architecture and training; init only differs
claims.evidence_quote: For image classification, expanding a 1M-parameter core to initialize an 85M-parameter ViT-Base improves I MA GE N ET top-1 accuracy by 2.2 pp over standard random initialization.

numbers.what: Zero-shot segmentation ImageNet-S mAP random init vs Procedural Core
numbers.quote: In ViTs, we localize a key benefit in the suppression of high-norm tokens that produces substantial improvements in zero-shot segmentation (I MAGE N ET-S mAP 32.3 → 42.9)

numbers.what: Gain vs random init across target depth
numbers.quote: Figure 5c shows that the Procedural Core outperforms the default random initialization at every tested depth, with the gain increasing from +2.0% at 6 layers to +2.8% at 24 layers.

survey_notes: Not a looped model at deployment; looping is a training-time compression/regularizer whose weights are then untied (inverse of retrofitting dense to looped). Supports the Block-Recurrent Hypothesis line that ViT computation is compressible into a few reused blocks; useful for the 'what looping buys in vision' discussion (transferable structure, not test-time compute).

title: Recurrent-Depth VLA: Implicit Test-Time Compute Scaling of Vision-Language-Action Models via Latent Iterative Reasoning
relevance_reason: Huginn-style prelude / weight-tied recurrent core / coda action head for a VLA, trained with randomized recurrence and TBPTT, with KL-based adaptive stopping.
one_sentence: Adds a Huginn-style recurrent action head (prelude, tied core with input injection, coda) on a Qwen2.5-0.5B VLA; LIBERO success climbs from 8.4% at 1 iteration to 92.6% at 8, with KL-convergence early stopping.
key_contributions: First VLA with weight-tied recurrent latent action head; noisy scratchpad init plus persistent input injection via concat adapter.
Training with Poisson log-normal sampled depth (mean 32) and TBPTT through last 8 iterations.
Adaptive stopping on KL/MSE between consecutive iterations; task-dependent iteration counts emerge; adaptive horizon execution.

setup.model_sizes: 0.5B (Qwen2.5-0.5B MiniVLA backbone) plus recurrent action head
setup.train_tokens_or_data: LIBERO and CALVIN robot demonstrations; real-world tasks
setup.loops_train: N ~ Poisson(e^tau)+1 with mu_rec = 32; TBPTT last 8 iterations
setup.baselines: End-to-end VLAs (OpenVLA, pi0, pi0.5), token-reasoning VLAs (ECoT, Fast-ThinkAct, 7B), same model at fewer iterations
setup.benchmarks: LIBERO (Spatial, Object, Goal, Long), CALVIN ABC->D, real robot

claims.claim: Test-time recurrence scaling: LIBERO average success rises log-linearly with iterations and saturates around 8-12.
claims.regime: same model, varying test-time iterations (no non-looped matched baseline)
claims.evidence_quote: Starting from near-random performance at Ninf = 1 (8.4% average), the model achieves substantial gains at each doubling of compute: 40.5% at Ninf = 2 (382% increase), 84.1% at Ninf = 4 (108% increase), and 92.6% at Ninf = 8 (10% increase).

claims.claim: KL-based adaptive stopping matches fixed-depth peak with 34% fewer iterations.
claims.regime: same model, adaptive vs fixed iterations
claims.evidence_quote: the Binary Adaptation strategy achieves 92.5% success rate (comparable to the 93.0% peak of fixed recurrence at N = 12) using an average of only k̄ = 7.93 iterations, which is a 34% reduction in compute.

claims.claim: RD-VLA (0.5B) beats prior VLAs including 7B token-reasoning methods on LIBERO; comparison against public models with different backbones/data.
claims.evidence_quote: RD-VLA achieves state-of-the-art performance of 93.0% with fixed recurrence, significantly outperforming all prior methods, including the strong Fast-ThinkAct baseline (89.7%).

claims.claim: Depth generalization is bounded: beyond an optimal iteration count, recurrence can saturate or degrade.
claims.evidence_quote: extending recurrence beyond this number of iterations may lead to state saturation or performance degradation rather than continued refinement.

numbers.what: CALVIN ABC->D average chain length
numbers.quote: RD-VLA achieves the highest average chain length of 3.39, outperforming OpenVLA [22] (3.27) and all other baselines.

numbers.what: Inference speedup over prior reasoning VLAs
numbers.quote: replacing token-based reasoning with latent reasoning to achieve constant memory usage and up to 80× inference speedup over prior reasoning-based VLA models.

numbers.what: Adaptive exits per task category (tau=1e-4)
numbers.quote: Spatial tasks require more iterations (µ = 11.8) than Object (µ = 9.8)

limitations: Small 0.5B backbone; depth extrapolation beyond the optimal iteration count saturates or degrades; adaptive intervention design space unexplored.
survey_notes: Direct transfer of the Huginn recipe (prelude/core/coda, noisy state init, input injection, log-normal Poisson depth sampling, truncated BPTT, KL-based exit) to robotics; reproduces the LM pattern of saturating gains and limited extrapolation. No iso-param or iso-FLOP non-recurrent head baseline; all cross-model claims are unmatched.

title: Soft Mixture-of-Recursions: Going Deeper with Recursive Vision Transformers
relevance_reason: Recursive ViT that reuses shared intermediate blocks T times and softly mixes all recursion-step outputs per token.
one_sentence: SR-ViT groups intermediate DeiT blocks into coarse-to-fine recursive units, adds per-step linear step transforms and token-wise soft mixtures over all recursion outputs; ImageNet top-1 rises 79.83 to 82.48 from T=1 to 4 with +1.7M params.
key_contributions: Shows naive recursion in ViT helps at T=2 but drops below baseline at T=3; MoR-style hard depth selection also fails at T=3.
SoftMoR: token-wise learned weighted sum over all recursion-step outputs plus residual linear step transforms between steps.
Recursion depth as a scaling axis across ImageNet classification, COCO detection/instance segmentation, ADE20K segmentation.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: ImageNet-1K, DeiT protocol, 300 epochs from scratch
setup.baselines: DeiT-T/S/B, naive recursion, hard selection (MoR-style), recursive unit organizations

claims.claim: Recursion depth scales SR-ViT-S with near-constant parameters: top-1 79.83 (T=1) to 82.48 (T=4) with 1.7M extra parameters.
claims.evidence_quote: On ImageNet-1K, increasing recursion depth from 1 to 4 improves SR-ViT-S top-1 accuracy from 79.83% to 82.48% with only 1.7M additional parameters, outperforming the substantially larger DeiT-B while using approximately 27% of its parameters.

claims.claim: Against DeiT-B at slightly lower FLOPs, SR-ViT-S T=4 is more accurate at both 224 and 384 resolution.
claims.evidence_quote: Further increasing T to 4 raises the accuracy to 82.48% and 84.24% at 224 and 384, respectively, compared with 81.80% and 83.10% for DeiT-B, while still requiring slightly fewer FLOPs.

claims.claim: Naive recursion and MoR-style hard selection do not scale past T=2 in ViTs; using only the last (or selected) step's representation is the bottleneck.
claims.evidence_quote: When T is increased to 3, naive recursion drops to 79.17%, falling below the non-recursive baseline. This confirms that recursive reuse alone is not sufficient to reliably benefit from deeper computation.

numbers.what: Hard selection vs soft mixture at T=3 (SR-ViT-S top-1)
numbers.quote: However, when T is increased to 3, hard selection drops to 80.54%, while Soft Mixture continues to improve and reaches 82.45%.

numbers.what: Naive recursion coarse-to-fine T=2 top-1
numbers.quote: In contrast, the coarse-to-fine organization achieves the strongest result, improving ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy from 79.83% to 81.12%.

survey_notes: Argues token-level routing (MoR) transfers poorly to vision because visual tokens are processed jointly, not generated; replaces hard routing with soft aggregation over steps (a DenseNet-like history injection). Agrees with Looped-DiT (2609.40305) and Training Crossroads (2608.04879) that naive weight-tied depth stops helping in vision without intermediate-step usage/supervision. No iso-effective-depth deep untied baseline.

title: Training-Free Hidden-State Refinement for Flow-Matching Image Generators
relevance_reason: Training-free repetition of selected frozen DiT layers (damped residual updates, K rounds) inside each denoising call of flow-matching T2I models.
one_sentence: Repeats each layer in a mid-to-late range of a frozen flow-matching DiT K times with step size 1/K, gated to early sampling progress, plus 'Loop Guidance' extrapolating looped vs ordinary velocity; beats extra sampling steps at equal or lower time.
key_contributions: Damped per-layer residual looping (eta = 1/K) for frozen DiTs; dense and sparse-token variants; sampling-progress gating and layer-range selection.
Loop Guidance: CFG-like extrapolation between looped and ordinary vector fields.
Wall-clock comparison: internal looping beats adding outer Euler steps at equal or lower generation time.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: none (training-free)
setup.loops_test: K = 4 default over layers [12, 27]; loop active for sampling progress in [0, 0.5]
setup.baselines: Same frozen models without looping, with 25/35/50 outer Euler steps
setup.benchmarks: GenEval, DPG-Bench, ImageReward, CLIP, OpenCLIP, PickScore

claims.claim: Internal layer looping at 25 steps beats a 50-step no-loop baseline on GenEval and DPG while being faster (wall-clock).
claims.regime: iso_param (same frozen weights); approximately iso-latency (lower time)
claims.evidence_quote: 0.8007 DPG-Bench in 2.1812 s, outperforming the 50-step no-loop baseline (0.4742 and 0.7738) while remaining faster than its 2.4032 s runtime.

claims.claim: Loop Guidance improves both primary metrics on all three frozen generators.
claims.evidence_quote: Loop Guidance further improves both primary metrics across all three tested models; on Scale-RAE DiT2.4B, it raises GenEval from 0.4471 to 0.5691 and DPG-Bench from 0.7656 to 0.8053.

claims.claim: Without guidance, transfer to RAEv2 is mixed (GenEval slightly drops); moderate K captures most gains and middle-to-late layers are better than early ones.
claims.evidence_quote: On RAEv2, both variants improve DPG-Bench and all auxiliary metrics but slightly reduce GenEval, so the unguided transfer result is mixed.

numbers.what: Sparse Token Loop time reduction vs Dense Token Loop
numbers.quote: Specifically, Sparse Token Loop reduces generation time by 22.6% on DiT2.4B and 39.6% on DiT9.8B relative to Dense Token Loop.

numbers.what: RAEv2 with Loop Guidance
numbers.quote: On RAEv2, Loop Guidance raises GenEval from 0.3829 to 0.4532 and DPGBench from 0.7131 to 0.7521 while improving every auxiliary metric.

limitations: Unguided transfer to RAEv2 mixed; guidance scale not tuned exhaustively; sparse variant slower at small (615M) scale.
survey_notes: Vision analogue of training-free layer repetition in LLMs; the damped step eta=1/K is a key difference from naive repetition (full updates cause excessive displacement). Agrees with Looped-DiT (2609.40305) that loop depth beats extra denoising steps under matched cost, here without any training and at 2.4B-9.8B. Middle-to-late layers best, consistent with LLM layer-duplication findings.

title: RecRec: Recursive Refinement for Sequential Recommendation
relevance_reason: TRM-style shared recursive core with inner/outer loops refining a persistent user-preference latent state, with a gated evidence-anchored correction.
one_sentence: RecRec refines a user-preference state with a weight-shared MLP core (T=7 outer steps x n=3 inner loops), a sigmoid gate interpolating back to the encoded history, and step-wise supervision; 3.9M-14M params beat SASRec, ReaRec and 7B LLM recommenders.
key_contributions: Recursive latent preference inference for sequential recommendation, inspired by TRM.
Evidence-anchored correction gate (interpolates refined state with original interaction encoding) to prevent drift.
Shows a peak in recursion steps (T=7) and that deeper unshared MLPs overfit.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: Three benchmark datasets incl. Steam, Luxury Beauty, Video Games (leave-one-out)
setup.baselines: SASRec, UniRec, LightGCN, NGCF, ReaRec; LLM recommenders ALLMRec, TallRec (7B), GPT4Rec

claims.claim: Recursion depth helps up to T=7 then degrades (over-refinement), mirroring LM overthinking.
claims.regime: iso_param (same model, varied T at training)
claims.evidence_quote: Increasing 𝑇 leads to consistent performance gains, with HR@1 peaking at 𝑇 = 7 (HR@1: 0.59). Beyond this point, performance degrades (e.g., HR@1 drops to 0.55 at 𝑇 = 13), indicating over-refinement.

claims.claim: Increasing unique depth of the core MLP beyond 5 layers overfits; recursion is the more parameter-efficient depth source.
claims.regime: unclear (deeper unshared core vs recursion, not FLOP-matched)
claims.evidence_quote: Increasing the depth to 10 layers (21.1M parameters) degrades performance (HR@1: 0.55), indicating overfitting to dataset-specific patterns rather than improved generalization.

claims.claim: RecRec beats sequential, graph, recursion-based and 7B LLM recommenders with far fewer parameters; baselines are separately configured models.
claims.evidence_quote: Remarkably, RecRec surpasses LLM-based models like ALLMRec and GPT4Rec despite a 99% smaller footprint (3.9M vs. 7B).

numbers.what: HR@1 on Steam at T=1 (single pass) vs T=7
numbers.quote: Our analysis on the Steam dataset shows that at 𝑇 = 1, RecRec reduces to a single-pass architecture (HR@1: 0.49).

survey_notes: Recsys transfer of TRM recipe (inner/outer recursion, deep supervision, state gating to input). Like LM looped models, gains peak then decline with more steps. Unlike LoopCTR (2604.19550), RecRec trains and tests at one fixed T and offers no FLOP-matched comparison.

title: LARES: Latent Reasoning for Sequential Recommendation
relevance_reason: Huginn-style pre-block plus recurrent core-block Transformer for sequential recommendation, with randomized log-normal Poisson depth, alignment pretraining and RL post-training.
one_sentence: LARES applies a recurrent core block (random-noise initial thought, input injection, LayerNorm) to all item tokens of a sequential recommender, samples depth from a log-normal Poisson in training, and adds trajectory/step alignment SSL plus GRPO-style RL post-training.
key_contributions: Depth-recurrent latent reasoning for sequential recommendation that refines all input tokens each step (vs last-token reasoning in ReaRec).
Self-supervised pretraining with trajectory-level and step-level alignment, then reinforcement post-training.
Plug-in compatibility with existing SR backbones (e.g., TedRec).

setup.model_sizes: pre-block and core-block each 1-2 Transformer layers; hidden size 256, embedding 64
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Four real-world datasets (incl. Amazon Instrument, Scientific)
setup.loops_train: k ~ Poisson(e^xi)+1 with mean k-bar+1, k-bar in {3,4,6}, truncated at 3 k-bar
setup.baselines: GRU4Rec, BERT4Rec, SASRec, FMLP-Rec, CL4SRec, DuoRec, BSARec, ERL/PRL/PRL++ (ReaRec family)

claims.claim: More reasoning steps help up to an optimum (3-4) and then degrade, analogous to overthinking.
claims.evidence_quote: performance initially improves with more reasoning steps but declines after reaching an optimal point, which is in line with the findings in ReaRec.

claims.claim: At comparable FLOPs (LARES 2+2x4 layers vs 10-layer SASRec), LARES adds about 10% latency; only latency, not accuracy, is reported at matched FLOPs.
claims.evidence_quote: The additional inference latency introduced by LARES remains moderate—approximately 10% higher than SASRec at comparable FLOPs.

claims.claim: LARES beats non-reasoning and reasoning SR baselines on four datasets; baselines use shared hyperparameters but are distinct architectures.
claims.regime: unmatched (shared embedding/hidden sizes, different architectures and compute)
claims.evidence_quote: Our proposed framework LARES outperforms all baselines, including both non-reasoning and reasoning models, by a large margin across all evaluation metrics on four datasets.

numbers.what: Optimal mean reasoning steps
numbers.quote: The optimal reasoning steps are 4 for Instrument and 3 for Scientific, highlighting the importance of selecting an appropriate reasoning depth for optimal performance.

numbers.what: Gain from plugging LARES into TedRec
numbers.quote: the superior TedRec model benefits from our framework, showing average improvements of 10.9% and 7.9% on the respective

limitations: Fixed reasoning depth for all sequences; excessive steps waste compute and can hurt; adaptive depth left to future work.
survey_notes: Recsys port of Huginn: pre-block + core, noisy initial state, randomized log-normal Poisson depth. Interest-peak (overthinking) phenomenon agrees with RecRec (2607.10541) and ReaRec. Notable: RL post-training of a looped model outside language. No accuracy result at matched FLOPs against a deeper SASRec.

title: Revisiting Implicit Models: Sparsity Trade-offs Capability in Weight-tied Model for Vision Tasks
relevance_reason: Benchmarks plain weight-tied (looped) vision layers against DEQs and explicit models; proposes per-iteration distinct sparse masks on the tied weight.
one_sentence: Shows plain unrolled weight-tied ResNet/ViT-like models beat DEQ variants and similar explicit models on CIFAR/ImageNet under the same budget, and that distinct fixed random sparse masks per iteration raise tied-layer capacity; width matters more than tied depth.
key_contributions: Fair benchmark: weight-tied (finite unroll, BPTT) beats DEQ / phantom-gradient DEQ in accuracy and time on vision.
Multi-mask weight-tied layers: deterministic random binary masks per iteration diversify a single tied weight.
Guidelines: increase width not tied depth; tied depth 6-8 is enough; wider and sparser preferred.

setup.model_sizes: Small and large ResNet-like and CCT/ViT-like models
setup.train_tokens_or_data: CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet32, ImageNet
setup.loops_train: tied depth e.g. 8 (DEQ comparison); 2-12 in trade-off study
setup.baselines: DEQ, phantom-gradient DEQ, explicit ResNet-20, CCT-7, dropout, same-mask sparse tied

claims.claim: Finite unrolled weight-tied models outperform DEQ variants and similarly structured explicit models in accuracy and time.
claims.regime: same structure and hyperparameters as DEQ; same data
claims.evidence_quote: the weight-tied model could outperform most of the latest DEQ variants as well as explicit models in both performance and time complexity across various neural architectures.

claims.claim: Increasing tied depth helps far less than increasing width; a 12-deep tied model lags a 2-deep one that is 2x wider.
claims.regime: varied depth/width at fixed mask density (not FLOP matched)
claims.evidence_quote: a 12-depth multi-mask weight-tied model significantly lags behind a 2-depth multi-mask weight-tied which is 2 times wider.

numbers.what: Recommended tied depth
numbers.quote: Practical guide #1: The model width matters, rather than the depth of weight-tied layers: practically it is sufficient to use a depth of 6 or 8 in the weight-tied layers to ensure reasonably good performance.

survey_notes: Supports 'finite unroll beats fixed-point/implicit training' in vision, consistent with LM findings favoring BPTT over implicit gradients. Per-iteration random masks are an early form of relaxed sharing (step-specific parameters with zero extra params). Its 'width beats tied depth' guideline is a counterpoint to vision papers claiming recursion as a scaling axis (2607.00774).

title: Looped Actor: Depth-Recurrent Reasoning Models for Reinforcement Learning
relevance_reason: FPRM-style fixed-point looped transformer policy with KL-stabilization halting, trained with standard online/offline RL objectives through executed loops.
one_sentence: Looped Actor adapts the Fixed-Point Reasoning Model to RL policies, halting when consecutive action distributions' KL falls below a threshold; at 0.5M params it beats a 16x larger untied iso-FLOP stack on Boxoban and Rush Hour and ties it on OGBench.
key_contributions: Complexity-theoretic MDP family where state-adaptive policies need asymptotically less expected compute than any optimal fixed-runtime policy.
Looped transformer actor (and looped critic) with KL-based halting, trained with standard RL treating halting as non-differentiable.
Iso-parameter and iso-FLOP (16 untied blocks) baselines across 22 tasks in six environments; probes show plans emerge over loops.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: Online RL (Boxoban, Rush Hour) and offline goal-conditioned RL (OGBench, 4 environments)
setup.baselines: Iso-Parameters (block applied once), Iso-FLOPs (16 untied blocks), DRC(3,3)

claims.claim: On planning-heavy puzzles, the 0.5M Looped Actor substantially outperforms an untied 16-block iso-FLOP baseline with 16x more parameters and DRC; the iso-parameter single-pass baseline barely learns.
claims.regime: iso_param and iso_train_flop / iso_effective_depth (16 untied blocks at max loops)
claims.evidence_quote: We report the success rate as a function of environment steps for Boxoban in Figure 1 and Rush Hour in Figure 2, showing the mean and standard deviation across three random seeds. Looped Actor substantially outperforms the Iso-FLOPs and DRC baselines despite having 2 to 16 times less

claims.claim: On less planning-heavy offline goal-conditioned control, Looped Actor ties or slightly beats the iso-FLOP baseline.
claims.evidence_quote: Looped Actor ties or slightly outperforms Iso-FLOPs in all four environments. Iso-Parameters performs substantially worse, achieving zero success on at least one downstream task in three of the four environments.

claims.claim: Compute allocation is structured: loops increase with remaining pushes and future optimal pushes become linearly decodable over loops.
claims.evidence_quote: For the Boxoban environment, we find that the computation allocation is structured: the number of loops increases with the number of remaining pushes and future optimal pushes become increasingly predictable from the latent state over successive loops.

numbers.what: Boxoban success vs untied 16x larger baseline
numbers.quote: On Boxoban, it achieves roughly twice the success rate of an untied transformer with 16 times as many parameters, while matching this baseline’s average performance across 20 offline goal-conditioned control tasks.

numbers.what: Model sizes
numbers.quote: We choose the hidden dimension of the blocks to be 128, resulting in a total of 0.5M parameters for Looped Actor and Iso-Parameters, and around 8M parameters for Iso-FLOPs.

limitations: No guarantee the learned policy is compute-optimal; computation is within a single environment step, no reasoning state carried across steps (memory/partial observability open).
survey_notes: Cleanest RL evidence with both iso-param and iso-FLOP (iso-effective-depth) baselines. Looped beats untied deeper model on planning tasks (generalization/data-efficiency advantage of tying, consistent with algorithmic-task results in LM literature) and ties elsewhere. Note the 'Iso-FLOPs' baseline matches compute only at max loops; with adaptive halting, Looped Actor uses fewer FLOPs.

title: Depth through recurrence: Looped transformers for flow-matching TTS
relevance_reason: Controlled comparison of seven weight-reuse layouts (cycle, sequence, prefix/middle/suffix partial loops) at matched executed depth in F5-TTS.
one_sentence: Trains seven F5-TTS Small layouts with 18 block calls each; SEQUENCE (each of 9 blocks applied twice consecutively) keeps WER competitive at 47.1% fewer params, more sharing hurts, and placement of the shared segment matters most at few sampling steps.
key_contributions: Iso-effective-depth (18 calls) comparison of sharing amount, order (cycle vs sequence) and placement (prefix/middle/suffix) in flow-matching TTS.
Interaction between loop layout and sampling budget: prefix vs suffix similar at 32 steps but diverge at 4 steps.
Call-ablation shows unshared early calls are most removal-sensitive; shared interior calls are robust.

setup.model_sizes: Baseline 158.0M (18 unique blocks); CYCLE/SEQUENCE 9x2 83.6M; CYCLE 6x3 58.8M; Prefix/Middle/Suffix 108.4M
setup.train_tokens_or_data: LibriTTS (train-clean-100/360, train-other-500), 500k updates, one run per layout
setup.loops_train: 2 or 3 visits of shared segment; 18 executed calls
setup.benchmarks: Seed-TTS test-en, LibriSpeech-PC (WER via Whisper large-v3, SIM-o, UTMOS)

claims.claim: At matched executed depth (18 calls), SEQUENCE 9x2 matches the unshared baseline's WER with 47.1% fewer parameters (differences not significant; not equivalence).
claims.evidence_quote: SEQUENCE uses 83.6M parameters versus Baseline’s 158.0M, a 47.1% reduction, with the same 18 block calls. At 32 steps, its WER is 2.03/2.26% on Seed-TTS/LibriSpeech-PC versus Baseline’s 2.23/2.29% (Table 1).

claims.claim: More sharing has limits: cycling 6 blocks three times raises WER vs cycling 9 blocks twice.
claims.evidence_quote: CYCLE 9 × 2 has 32-step WER of 2.60/2.14%; CYCLE 6 × 3 saves another 24.8M parameters but raises WER to 2.96/2.65% and lowers SIM-o on both datasets.

claims.claim: Placement of the shared segment interacts with the sampling budget: suffix sharing is much worse at 4 steps.
claims.evidence_quote: At four steps, Suffix instead exceeds Prefix by 3.44 pp, 95% CI [2.77, 4.14], and 5.97 pp [3.69, 8.70].

numbers.what: Peak inference memory reduction from 9x2 sharing
numbers.quote: CYCLE 9 × 2 and SEQUENCE 9 × 2 reduce peak allocated memory from 877 to 574 MB (34.5%); CYCLE 6 × 3 and the partial loops use 474 and 675 MB.

numbers.what: Cycle vs sequence at matched size and depth (Seed-TTS 32-step WER)
numbers.quote: At matched size and depth, SEQUENCE lowers 32-step Seed-TTS WER from CYCLE’s 2.60 to 2.03, a paired change of −0.57 pp

limitations: One training run per layout (training-seed variance not measured); F5-TTS Small only; no visit-index embedding or auxiliary supervision tested; sampling time unchanged (no speedup).
survey_notes: Speech evidence that looping saves parameters/memory but not latency at matched executed depth. Cycle vs sequence (repeat-each-layer) order matters, echoing Takase & Kiyono in MT. Keeping early blocks unshared (sandwich) matters, consistent with LM prelude findings. Careful statistics (paired CIs) make it a reliable iso-effective-depth data point.

title: DeepJEPA: Scaling World Models from Within
relevance_reason: Weight-tied recurrent transition cell inside a JEPA world model with a learned per-candidate, per-step continue head for adaptive internal depth during CEM planning.
one_sentence: DeepJEPA makes each imagined JEPA transition a weight-tied recurrent computation (Kmax=4) with a learned halting head supervised by marginal latent-error reduction; uniformly deeper transitions never beat K=1, but adaptive depth (mean 1.00-1.26) matches or beats every fixed depth.
key_contributions: Identifies transition-level internal depth as a test-time scaling axis for world-model planners, framed as value of computation.
Learned continue head per candidate-time pair trained from marginal prediction-error reduction, reward-free.
Shows uniform depth is non-monotonic; useful extra updates concentrate at contact events and act through CEM elite-set reordering.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: Offline visual-control data for Reacher, Cube Single/Double/Triple, PushT
setup.loops_test: fixed K = 1-4 or learned halting with threshold eta
setup.baselines: Fixed-depth K=1..4 from same recurrent checkpoint family; non-recurrent LeWM
setup.benchmarks: Reacher, Cube Single, Cube Double, Cube Triple, PushT (success rate, CEM MPC)

claims.claim: Uniformly deeper transitions are not a scaling law: fixed K=4 never beats K=1 in aggregate across five settings.
claims.regime: iso_param (same checkpoint, roots, CEM seeds), varying test depth
claims.evidence_quote: Within the same recurrent checkpoint family, aggregate fixed K = 4 never exceeds fixed K = 1: it is lower on Reacher, Cube Single, and PushT, and tied on Cube Double and Cube Triple.

claims.claim: Learned adaptive depth improves or matches the best fixed depth while averaging near one update per transition.
claims.regime: iso_param; fewer FLOPs than deeper fixed settings; thresholds selected on the evaluation sweep
claims.evidence_quote: Across five visual-control settings, DeepJEPA improves or matches the strongest fixed-depth planner while averaging only 1.00–1.26 updates per transition.

claims.claim: A non-recurrent baseline (LeWM) still wins on one setting; gains are small (0.9-3.3 points) and thresholds are chosen on the evaluation sweep.
claims.evidence_quote: Cube Double separates the comparisons: adaptive depth improves its recurrent family from 72.7% to 74.0%, while LeWM obtains 74.7%.

numbers.what: Gains over best fixed depth at mean depth
numbers.value: Reacher +1.3 at 1.03; Cube Triple +3.3 at 1.22; PushT +0.9 at 1.02
numbers.quote: Reacher gains 1.3 points over its best fixed mean at K̄ = 1.03, Cube Triple gains 3.3 points at K̄ = 1.22, and PushT gains 0.9 points at K̄ = 1.02.

limitations: Halting thresholds chosen from the evaluation sweep, not held-out; mean depth does not translate to wall-clock savings under batched execution; PushT success low; probes use one checkpoint per task.
survey_notes: Important negative result outside language: in world-model planning, fixed extra recurrent depth does not help (contrast with RD-VLA 2602.07845 and Looped Actor 2609.37432 where more loops help); value comes only from sparse, learned allocation. Gains small and threshold selection optimistic.

title: Recursive Scaling in Masked Diffusion Models
relevance_reason: Applies a shared K-layer denoising block L times inside each masked-diffusion denoising step, with step embeddings and loop-wise supervision.
one_sentence: R-MDMs loop a shared block L times per masked-diffusion step; at fixed params and at matched effective depth (iso-FLOP) recursion matches or beats 5-10x larger deeper models on Sudoku/Countdown, helps most at few denoising steps, and entropy-guided two-axis decoding improves the quality-NFE frontier.
key_contributions: Recursion as a second test-time axis in MDMs, distinct from denoising steps: loops refine marginals at a fixed masked state; steps commit tokens.
Iso-param and iso-effective-depth (KL x 1 vs K x L) comparisons with learned step embedding and loop-averaged masked CE supervision.
Dependence-fidelity error decomposition and entropy-guided adaptive loop stopping plus commit rules across Sudoku, Countdown, RNA, TinyGSM.

setup.model_sizes: e.g. 10.8M (6x5 Sudoku) vs 53.1M deeper baseline; TinyGSM 161M
setup.train_tokens_or_data: Sudoku 1.8M 9x9 and 100k 25x25 boards; Countdown 100k per operand count; RNA sequences; TinyGSM
setup.loops_test: Ls may differ from Lt; entropy-based stopping
setup.baselines: Single-pass K x 1 (iso-param), KL x 1 deeper (iso-FLOP / iso-effective-depth)
setup.benchmarks: Sudoku VPR, Countdown RTR, RNA Delta-Z, GSM8K execution accuracy

claims.claim: At fixed parameters, more loops improve quality, especially at small denoising budgets.
claims.evidence_quote: For example, on Countdown-3 at T =10, L=3 reaches 92.4% RTR, compared with 59.4% for the single-pass model.

claims.claim: At matched effective depth and gradient updates, recursion matches or beats non-recursive baselines with L-times fewer parameters.
claims.regime: iso_effective_depth / iso_infer_flop, same data and updates
claims.evidence_quote: Recursion matches or outperforms the deeper baselines: on Sudoku at T =5, (6 ⊗ 5) achieves 93.6% VPR with 10.8M parameters versus 77.8% with 53.1M

claims.claim: Recursion gives benefit beyond added depth: increasing loops helps more than increasing unique layers at T=40.
claims.evidence_quote: at T =40, increasing Sudoku depth from 18 to 30 layers raises VPR only 96.6% → 97.2%, whereas increasing L from 1 to 5 at depth 6 gives 95.8% → 98.0%.

claims.claim: Best recursive models exceed the non-recursive baseline across all four domains, including executable math at 161M.
claims.evidence_quote: The best recursive result exceeds the non-recursive baseline in every domain: Sudoku from 80.7% to 100% VPR, Countdown-4 from 50.0% to 82.0% RTR, RNA from ∆Z = 0.453 to 0.140

numbers.what: 25x25 Sudoku at 90% masking, T=100
numbers.quote: at 90% masking and T =100, VPR rises from 2.0% to 52.2% with L=3 (Appendix G.4).

numbers.what: TinyGSM accuracy and evaluation cost with fixed-entropy commit at L=3
numbers.quote: on TinyGSM, fixed entropy at L=3 matches the best fixed uniform accuracy (24.0% vs. 24.2%) with 69 instead of 768 evaluations

limitations: Structured tasks only; open-ended language generation and larger scale untested; recursion cannot remove dependence error among jointly committed tokens.
survey_notes: Strong controlled evidence (iso-param and iso-effective-depth) in discrete diffusion; same conclusion as Looped-DiT (2609.40305) for continuous diffusion: loops are a separate axis from sampling steps and most valuable at low step budgets. Uses step embedding plus deep supervision, consistent with LM recipes. Also relevant to the language/diffusion-LM section.

title: FlexLoop: Depth-Elastic Looped Policies for Adaptive Test-Time Computation in Deep RL
relevance_reason: Post-training of depth-recurrent (IRU) RL policies so that shallower recurrent depths become usable, with consistency-based adaptive depth.
one_sentence: Finds fixed-depth looped RL policies (IRU) are reliable only near their training depth; FlexLoop post-trains with the original RL loss plus adjacent-depth self-distillation, enabling consistency-based early stopping that cuts average depth up to 43%.
key_contributions: Identifies recurrent-depth specialization in looped RL policies trained at a fixed depth.
Post-training: continue original RL objective (keeps full-depth capability and OOD generalization) plus progressive deeper-to-shallower policy distillation.
State-wise adaptive inference from consistency between successive depths; up to 1.34x wall-clock speedup.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: 30 online and offline long-horizon goal-conditioned environments (e.g. BoxPick, LightsOut), discrete and continuous actions
setup.loops_train: pretrained at full depth K (e.g. IRU-5), then elastic post-training
setup.baselines: Pretrained fixed-depth IRU; Self-TD only; Distill only; AnyK-TD (joint all-depth TD)
setup.benchmarks: Success rate, average recurrent depth, wall-clock

claims.claim: Looped RL policies trained at a fixed depth specialize to that depth; shallower depths fail, so computation cannot be reduced at deployment.
claims.evidence_quote: Surprisingly, we find that pretrained looped policies exhibit severe recurrent-depth specialization: reliable decisions are concentrated near the full trained depth, tying deployment computation to this depth even when less computation may suffice.

claims.claim: Jointly training all depths (AnyK-TD) hurts full-depth capability or OOD generalization, and distillation alone hurts generalization; combining continued RL with adjacent-depth distillation works.
claims.evidence_quote: naively training these depths jointly suppresses full-depth performance, while relying on distillation alone can degrade generalization to unseen tasks.

claims.claim: Adaptive depth reduces average recurrent depth by up to 43% with competitive or better performance.
claims.evidence_quote: Keeping competitive performance, FlexLoop reduces average recurrent depth by up to 43% and achieves up to 1.34× wall-clock speedup in a stress test.

limitations: Only IRU-style recurrent policies; transformer-based looped policies and better halting criteria left to future work.
survey_notes: RL analogue of the LM 'trained-depth specialization / no free early exit' finding; the remedy (self-distillation from deeper to shallower loops) mirrors ELT and LoopFormer-style elastic training. Contrast with RD-VLA (2602.07845) where randomized depth during training gives elasticity from the start.

title: LoopCTR: Unlocking the Loop Scaling Power for Click-Through Rate Prediction
relevance_reason: Sandwich (entry / shared loop block / exit) CTR Transformer with hyper-connected residuals, MoE in the loop, and per-loop process supervision.
one_sentence: LoopCTR loops a MoE-augmented, hyper-connected Transformer block up to 3 times during CTR training with supervision at every loop depth, so even zero-loop inference beats all baselines; looped beats an iso-FLOP stacked variant on all four datasets.
key_contributions: Loop scaling for CTR: train-multi-loop, infer-zero-loop via process supervision at every loop depth.
Loop block with input-dependent hyper-connected residuals (multi-stream mixing, zero-init dynamic terms) and MoE to overcome shared-layer expressiveness bottleneck.
Iso-FLOP StackCTR comparison and oracle per-sample loop-depth analysis (0.013-0.023 AUC headroom).

setup.train_tokens_or_data: Amazon (3M interactions), KuaiVideo, TaobaoAds (25M), InHouse (nine days of Alibaba production logs)
setup.baselines: DNN CTR models (DIN etc.), HSTU, OneTrans, MTGR, StackCTR (3 unshared layers, iso-FLOP)

claims.claim: At identical FLOPs, the shared-weight loop beats a stacked unshared counterpart in AUC on all four datasets (small margins on some).
claims.regime: iso_infer_flop / iso_effective_depth (StackCTR uses 3 distinct layers), iso_data
claims.evidence_quote: Comparing LoopCTR(3/3) with StackCTR under identical FLOPs reveals a clear advantage for weight sharing: LoopCTR(3/3) leads on AUC across all four datasets (0.8726 vs. 0.8690 on Amazon; 0.7002 vs. 0.6999 on InHouse).

claims.claim: More training loops raise AUC, but extra inference loops give diminishing returns; first inference loop gives most of the gain.
claims.evidence_quote: Increasing L from 0 to 3 consistently raises AUC across all datasets (e.g., 0.8662→0.8728 on Amazon, 0.6966→0.7007 on InHouse), confirming that deeper loop scaling consistently improves model quality.

claims.claim: Zero-loop inference after multi-loop training beats all baselines at a fraction of their FLOPs and latency (baselines are different architectures).
claims.evidence_quote: On InHouse, LoopCTR(0/3) achieves the best AUC with only 13.38M FLOPs and 9.26ms latency, while HSTU requires 2150M FLOPs / 775.72ms and OneTrans requires 417.97M FLOPs / 494.58ms (Appendix Table 6).

claims.claim: Per-sample oracle loop depth reveals large headroom, and models trained with fewer loops have higher oracle ceilings.
claims.evidence_quote: Post-hoc oracle selection of the optimal loop depth per sample uncovers 0.013–0.023 AUC of untapped performance over the best realized LoopCTR(i/3) result across datasets.

numbers.what: Inference-loop curve on Amazon (L=3)
numbers.quote: On Amazon with L=3, AUC rises from 0.8715 (i=0) to 0.8728 (i=1) but plateaus at 0.8728 (i=2) and slightly dips to 0.8726 (i=3).

limitations: Oracle headroom not yet realized by any adaptive policy; StackCTR occasionally matches or beats LoopCTR (TaobaoAds).
survey_notes: Distinctive: looping as a training-time regularizer whose benefit is distilled into the shared weights so inference uses zero loops (cf. Procedural Core 2609.37631 using recurrence only for init). Flatter minima explanation. Regularization benefit is plausible in sparse-data recsys; contrast with LM where loops are needed at inference.

title: MPCoT: Reward-Guided Multi-Path Latent Reasoning for Test-Time Scalable Vision-Language-Action
relevance_reason: Weight-tied refiner applied K times to M parallel latent action hypotheses (with context injection) before an unchanged VLA action head.
one_sentence: MPCoT adds to OpenVLA-OFT a shared residual refiner run for K steps over M parallel latent hypotheses, softly aggregated by a scorer trained with reward signals; depth and width each add a few points on CALVIN/LIBERO at ms-level latency.
key_contributions: Depth-width latent deliberation module (K weight-tied steps x M hypotheses) for VLA with zero reasoning tokens.
Training-only reward-guided path preference (expert consistency, frozen Qwen3-VL progress, endpoint consistency).
Depth/width sweep vs latency; real-world ALOHA Mini bimanual evaluation.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: LIBERO, CALVIN demonstrations; real ALOHA Mini tasks
setup.loops_test: K in 1-7, M in 1-6 without retraining
setup.baselines: OpenVLA-OFT (matched protocol), single-path latent CoT, textual CoT
setup.benchmarks: LIBERO, CALVIN, five ALOHA Mini tasks

claims.claim: Single-path depth helps then saturates: K from 1 to 5 raises CALVIN 5-step success 82.5 to 88.9; K=7 adds only 0.2.
claims.evidence_quote: With M = 1, increasing K from 1 to 5 raises CALVIN 3-step SR from 94.8% to 96.3% and 5-step SR from 82.5% to 88.9%. Moving to K = 7 adds 0.2 points on each metric for another 5 ms.

claims.claim: At equal latency, spending compute on width (parallel hypotheses) beats extra single-path depth.
claims.evidence_quote: At the same reported 38 ms, (5, 4) exceeds (7, 1) by 0.4 points on LIBERO-Long and 0.3 on both CALVIN metrics. Width thus contributes beyond extra single-path depth at this latency.

claims.claim: Authors state that no baseline jointly matched for parameters and compute was run.
claims.evidence_quote: Component ablations also do not replace a baseline jointly matched for parameters and compute.

numbers.what: Real-world ALOHA Mini average success vs OpenVLA-OFT
numbers.quote: On five real-world ALOHA Mini bimanual tasks, average success increases from 71.3% to 82.0% over the matched OpenVLAOFT baseline.

numbers.what: Real-robot policy-query latency
numbers.quote: OpenVLA-OFT and MPCoT average 364 and 465 ms per query (+101 ms) over 100 queries on the same NVIDIA A100 GPU.

limitations: Single training seed; one embodiment, 30 trials per task; Qwen3-VL label bias; no baseline jointly matched for parameters and compute.
survey_notes: Adds the width (parallel latent paths) axis to looped VLA heads; at matched latency width > depth, echoing parallel-loop ideas in LMs. Depth saturation at K about 5-7 consistent with RD-VLA's 8-12. Evidence regime weak (unmatched; acknowledged).

title: HRM-Agent: Training a recurrent reasoning model in dynamic environments using reinforcement learning
relevance_reason: HRM (two-timescale recurrent modules) trained with DQN only, with the recurrent latent carried across environment time-steps.
one_sentence: Adapts HRM to RL with a DQN head, trains it on dynamic four-rooms and random-maze navigation (~99% goal reach), and shows carrying the converged recurrent state to the next time-step speeds convergence, indicating reuse of earlier computation.
key_contributions: First HRM variant trained only by RL (DQN, epsilon-greedy) in dynamic, partially changing mazes.
'Carry Z' vs 'Reset Z': initializing recurrent state from previous step's converged state.
Convergence-dynamics analysis showing plan reuse across environment steps.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: Four-rooms with doors and random maze environments (RL)
setup.loops_train: HRM recurrent cycles (ACT disabled for analysis)
setup.benchmarks: Goal-reach fraction, path length, convergence distance

claims.claim: HRM trained only with RL reaches the goal in about 99% of episodes in both dynamic maze environments.
claims.evidence_quote: The HRM-Agent model is able to reach the goal in approximately 99% of all episodes in both environments.

claims.claim: Carrying the recurrent latent across time-steps leads to faster convergence and more plan-consistent actions than resetting it.
claims.evidence_quote: In the Random Maze environment, the recurrent process converges faster with “Carry Z”, both when the environment has changed, and when it has not 6.

limitations: Small-scale grid environments; no comparison to non-recurrent or other RL baselines; gradients not propagated through recurrence (HRM one-step gradient).
survey_notes: Shows the HRM recipe (one-step gradient, two-timescale recurrence) trains under pure RL; carrying latent state across environment steps is a design choice absent from LM looping (cf. Looped Actor 2609.37432, which does not carry state). Evidence is qualitative; no matched baselines.

title: SPIN: An Empirical Evaluation on Sharing Parameters of Isotropic Networks
relevance_reason: Systematic design-space study of cross-layer weight sharing (sequential, strided/cycle, pyramid) in isotropic vision nets (ConvMixer, ConvNeXt, DeiT).
one_sentence: Explores sharing topology, lightweight dynamic transforms and weight-fusion initialization from pretrained unshared nets for isotropic CNN/ViT models; sequential (adjacent-layer) sharing plus fusion compresses ConvMixer about 1.9x at iso-FLOPs with no accuracy loss.
key_contributions: Framework of sharing topologies: sharing mapping (sequential vs strided/cycle) and distribution (uniform, pyramid, front).
Weight fusion initialization (e.g., channel-weighted mean of pretrained layers) to retrofit shared models from dense ones.
Iso-FLOP and iso-parameter comparisons on ImageNet for ConvMixer, ConvNeXt, DeiT.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: ImageNet
setup.loops_train: share rate 2 (groups of 2 sequential layers) and others
setup.baselines: Unshared iso-FLOP models, iso-parameter smaller models, prior weight-sharing methods

claims.claim: Adjacent-layer (sequential) and pyramid sharing work best at share rate 2, consistent with layer-wise similarity; other topologies lose more accuracy.
claims.evidence_quote: When share rate is 2, ConvMixer with uniform-sequential, middle-pyramid, and front-sequential sharing topology result in similar accuracy (2.5% less than the non-shared model) while other combinations result in lower accuracy.

claims.claim: With weight fusion, isotropic networks are compressed up to 2x without accuracy loss.
claims.evidence_quote: Our experiments show that, when applying these techniques, we can compress state-of-the-art isotropic networks by up to 2 times without losing any accuracy across many isotropic architectures.

claims.claim: For DeiT, weight sharing halves parameters within 1 point top-1, and beats unshared models at iso-parameters.
claims.evidence_quote: Compared to the baseline, the WS-DeiT-S model is able to get similar accuracy, within 1 point Top-1 with half the parameters. At iso-parameters, the WS-DeiT models significantly outperform non-weight-sharing models.

numbers.what: Share rates achieved at similar accuracy
numbers.quote: ConvMixer-768/32, ConvMixer156/20, and ConvNeXt-18 with weight sharing and weight fusion achieve 1.86x, 1.91x and 1.92 share rate while having a similar accuracy.

survey_notes: Vision counterpart of Takase & Kiyono: sequential (repeat-each-layer) sharing beats strided/cycle at share rate 2 for CNNs, matching the TTS result (2609.29768) where SEQUENCE beats CYCLE. Weight fusion from dense checkpoints is an early form of retrofitting shared models (cf. Relaxed Recursive Transformers init).

title: BA-T: An Iterative Transformer for Two-View Bundle Adjustment
relevance_reason: A single shared, BA-structured Transformer layer applied iteratively to latent camera and geometry tokens (iterative refinement with tied weights, output-state recurrence).
one_sentence: BA-T replaces deep cross-view decoder stacks with one bundle-adjustment-inspired layer reused for K iterations (camera update then geometry update), trained with increasing-weight iterative supervision; 38M params match or beat 113M-765M two-view/multi-view models.
key_contributions: Single reusable BA-inspired refinement layer alternating camera and local-geometry updates in latent space.
Iterative supervision with later iterations weighted more (train K=5, infer K=4).
Comparison with a size-matched stacked decoder trained iteratively (ViSTA-dagger w/ iterative training).

setup.train_tokens_or_data: Two-view 3D reconstruction training data (not detailed here)
setup.baselines: DUSt3R, MASt3R-like two-view models, VGGT and multi-view models, ViSTA-dagger (comparable decoder size), ViSTA-dagger w/ iterative training

claims.claim: Against a decoder of comparable size trained the same way, BA-T is better at every iteration; it cuts 3D correspondence error by 44% vs 27%.
claims.regime: approximately iso_param (comparable decoder size), same training
claims.evidence_quote: For comparison, ViSTA† [49] reduces 3D correspondence error by only 27%, whereas BA-T achieves 44%, showing that our BA-inspired design more effectively enforces reconstruction consistency.

claims.claim: Iterative gains saturate after 3-4 iterations.
claims.evidence_quote: Most improvements occur within the first 3–4 iterations (fig. 5), after which performance converges.

claims.claim: BA-T matches or beats much larger feed-forward reconstruction models (unmatched data and size).
claims.evidence_quote: Notably, it achieves this with a compact reusable layer (38M parameters), much smaller than prior methods (113M–765M), balancing accuracy and efficiency

survey_notes: Domain-specific looping: structure of the update (alternating camera/geometry) matters more than generic stacked attention; RAFT-like iterative refinement lineage rather than LM looping. Saturation at 3-4 iterations.

title: Looped World Models
relevance_reason: Parameter-shared looped transformer block with spectrally constrained state retention (negative-diagonal A, ZOH) and entropy-regularized exit gate for world modelling.
one_sentence: LoopWM loops a shared transformer block with contractive (Parcae-style) state retention and an entropy-regularized exit gate, plus 'deferred decoding' across rollout steps; a ~1B model is compared against closed API LLMs on text world-model benchmarks.
key_contributions: Claims first looped architecture for world modelling, borrowing spectral-norm-constrained state retention from Prairie et al. (2026).
Adaptive early exit with entropy regularization; deferred decoding keeps latent state across action steps.
Evaluation on ScienceWorld and AlfWorld text world-model tasks against API LLMs.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: ScienceWorld and AlfWorld world-modelling data (details not disclosed)
setup.baselines: claude-opus-4-6-max, gemini-3-flash-preview, qwen-3.5-flash and other API LLMs
setup.benchmarks: ScienceWorld, AlfWorld (EM, token F1, BLEU-4, entity)

claims.claim: A ~1B looped world model beats an API LLM on ScienceWorld EM by 21.2% relative; '100x parameter efficiency' is asserted relative to closed-source API models of undisclosed size.
claims.regime: unmatched (API LLMs, different data and training, sizes not public)
claims.evidence_quote: On average, our model shows a promising capability, clearly surpassing the baseline by 21.2% on EM, and clearly on other metrics.

claims.claim: Authors acknowledge selective disclosure; no non-looped matched baseline or loop ablation is reported in this version.
claims.evidence_quote: the current manuscript is intentionally selective in disclosure scope. In this version, our goal is to establish the core architectural thesis

limitations: Selective disclosure; no loop ablation or matched non-looped baseline; parameter-efficiency claim relative to API models of unknown size; continuous visual environments only mentioned (training loss reducible).
builds_on: Parcae / Prairie et al. 2026 (stable looped dynamics)
survey_notes: Weakest evidence in the RL/world-model cluster: headline '100x parameter efficiency' rests on comparison with closed API LLMs. Cite only as an existence example of borrowing the contractive state-retention parameterization; contrast with DeepJEPA (2610.00368), which finds uniform extra depth does not help world-model planning.

title: LoopTrack: A Simple Baseline for Parameter-Efficient Transformer Tracking
relevance_reason: One-stream visual tracker that loops 1-3 shared Transformer blocks K times with step embeddings, target-aware feedback, and cross-frame gated memory.
one_sentence: LoopTrack loops 1-3 shared Transformer blocks (K sampled 6-12 in training, 8 at test) with step embeddings, target-aware response feedback and gated cross-frame memory; 3.4M-6.4M params reach 66.2-69.3% SUC on LaSOT.
key_contributions: Parameter-shared looped one-stream tracker as a compact alternative to distillation-based lightweight trackers.
Target-aware looping (intermediate response maps fed back with step embeddings) and gated target memory across frames.
Randomized loop count during training (Beta-sampled K in 6..12) enabling flexible test-time depth.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: LaSOT, GOT-10k, TrackingNet, COCO training splits
setup.loops_train: K = 6 + round(6u), u ~ Beta(1,2), K in {6..12}
setup.baselines: Parameter-efficient trackers (UETrack-T/B etc.); fixed-K training ablation

claims.claim: Looped shared blocks give strong accuracy at very small parameter counts vs other efficient trackers (separately trained models).
claims.evidence_quote: LoopTrackOne , with a single shared Transformer block, achieves 66.2% SUC score on LaSOT with only 3.4M parameters, while LoopTrackThree , using three shared blocks, achieves 69.3% SUC score with 6.4M model parameters

claims.claim: Test-time loop count trades accuracy for speed; peak at K=8, no gain from deeper inference, K=4 (outside training range) still works.
claims.evidence_quote: Performance peaks at K = 8 with 69.3 SUC, while deeper inference provides no further gains. Despite lying outside the training range [6, 12], K = 4 still achieves 67.8 SUC at 151 FPS without retraining

claims.claim: Randomized loop-count training beats fixed-K training for the shared cell.
claims.evidence_quote: counts consistently improves over fixed-K training, supporting loop-count sampling for the

survey_notes: Vision tracker reproducing LM loop recipes: step embeddings, randomized depth in training, extrapolation to unseen (shallower) depth, gains saturating at training mean. No unshared iso-effective-depth baseline reported in main text.

title: Fixed-Point Masked Generative Modeling
relevance_reason: Replaces middle layers of masked diffusion/MaskGIT denoisers with a weight-shared fixed-point block solved iteratively, warm-started across denoising steps.
one_sentence: FP-MGMs replace middle denoiser layers with a shared fixed-point block trained by stochastic Jacobian-free backprop, add cross-step consistency loss and three-state warm-start reuse; on OWT CoFRe cuts params 38.8% and beats MDLM+SDTT at every forward-pass budget.
key_contributions: Fixed-point (DEQ-style) weight-shared block inside MDLM and MaskGIT denoisers; effective depth set by solver iterations.
Three-state reuse (3SR) warm-start: unchanged, still-masked and newly revealed tokens reuse previous fixed point differently; cross-step consistency loss.
Conversion of pretrained MDLM into FP-MDLM with short distillation (4% of pretraining steps).

setup.model_sizes: FP-MDLM 104M vs MDLM 170M; MaskGIT-Large vs FP-MaskGIT
setup.train_tokens_or_data: OpenWebText (seq 1024); ImageNette 256x256 (VQ tokens)
setup.loops_train: SJFB: Nng ~ U{0..4} no-grad + Ng ~ U{3..6} grad iterations
setup.loops_test: decreasing iteration schedule under fixed transformer-block budget (48-768 forward passes)
setup.benchmarks: Generative perplexity (GPT-2 Large), entropy, FID, IS, training time, VRAM

claims.claim: At matched transformer-block forward-pass budgets, CoFRe improves generative perplexity over MDLM+SDTT with fewer parameters.
claims.evidence_quote: For language, CoFRe improves generative perplexity over MDLM+SDTT at every reported budget, reducing from 193.1 to 101.8 at budget 96 and from 47.0 to 37.8 at budget 768.

claims.claim: On images, the fixed-point MaskGIT improves FID at every budget while halving training time and VRAM.
claims.evidence_quote: CoFRe improves FID over MaskGIT-Large at every reported budget, for example from 174.1 to 96.7 at budget 48 and from 30.0 to 22.8 at budget 384.

claims.claim: A pretrained MDLM can be converted to a fixed-point model with 4% of pretraining steps and beat the 1M-step FP-MDLM.
claims.evidence_quote: a pretrained MGM can be efficiently converted into a more compute-efficient FP architecture: improving over the 1M-step FP-MDLM baseline at every sampling budget, with only 4% of the original pretraining steps.

numbers.what: Resource savings vs MDLM on OWT
numbers.quote: On OpenWebText, CoFRe reduces parameters by 38.8%, training time by 11.5%, and VRAM by 16.9%, while improving generative perplexity from 830.8 to 101.8 at a budget of 96 transformer-block forward passes, compared to MDLM.

numbers.what: ImageNette training time and VRAM
numbers.quote: It also reduces training time from 17h46m to 9h08m and VRAM from 72.45 GiB to 35.74 GiB.

limitations: Gains partly from cross-step consistency (self-distillation), not only the fixed-point block; reported numbers are single points on a quality-diversity trade-off.
survey_notes: Fixed-point/DEQ variant of looping in discrete diffusion for text and images; warm-starting the loop state from the previous denoising step is a diffusion-specific state-passing choice (analogue of KV/state reuse across tokens). Concurrent with R-MDM (2606.18022), which uses plain unrolled loops; both find loops most useful at low sampling budgets. Note generative perplexity at low budgets can be gamed by low entropy; authors report entropy.

title: Training Crossroads for Recurrent Vision Transformers: Recurrence, Neural ODEs, and Deep Supervision
relevance_reason: Controlled study of a single-block recurrent ViT (bViT) vs standard ViT at matched FLOPs and matched parameters, plus ODE-solver and deep-supervision regimes.
one_sentence: On CIFAR-100, a single-block recurrent ViT loses to standard ViT at matched FLOPs but wins at matched parameters; ODE wrappers need the state-subtracted field; stage-wise deep supervision buys robustness beyond the training horizon at the cost of nominal accuracy.
key_contributions: Matched-FLOP vs matched-parameter comparison of bViT and ViT under a common protocol (3 runs, 200 epochs).
Neural-ODE view: state-subtracted vector field required (3-6 point penalty otherwise); higher-order solvers act as architectural bias, not numerical refinement.
Extrapolation: naive recurrence collapses to near-random beyond training horizon; stage-wise deep supervision degrades gracefully.

setup.model_sizes: small ViT/bViT on CIFAR-100 (grid over unique depth D and steps S)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: CIFAR-100, 200 epochs, 3 runs
setup.loops_test: training horizon and extrapolated horizons up to 192 evaluations
setup.baselines: Standard ViT (independent blocks), DEQ/Anderson and TRM-style supervision (reported unstable)

claims.claim: Recurrence is not a universal replacement for depth: standard ViT wins at matched FLOPs, bViT wins at matched parameter memory.
claims.regime: iso_infer_flop (ViT better); iso_param (bViT better); same data
claims.evidence_quote: Under matched computational budgets, the classical ViT remains preferable, as its independently parameterized blocks provide higher accuracy for a given FLOPs budget.

claims.claim: Accuracy saturates then slowly degrades with more recurrent steps, and collapses to near-random beyond the training horizon; deep supervision improves extrapolation robustness but not nominal accuracy.
claims.evidence_quote: Accuracy initially improves with additional recurrent steps, but eventually saturates and slowly degrades. When the same model is extrapolated beyond its training horizon, accuracy can collapse to near-random level.

claims.claim: Wrapping a residual block as an ODE vector field without subtracting the state costs 3-6 accuracy points; higher-order solvers do not uniformly help.
claims.evidence_quote: Table 1 shows that the statesubtracted formulation consistently outperforms the control by roughly 3–6 accuracy points—a nontrivial penalty for an error that is invisible at the API level of common ODE libraries.

limitations: CIFAR-100 only, small models; DEQ and TRM-style supervision found unstable in their setting.
survey_notes: Key contested-claim evidence: at iso-FLOP the untied ViT wins, at iso-param the looped ViT wins, the same regime split reported for LMs. Contradicts SoftMoR (2607.00774) style claims of recursion as a free scaling axis unless the regime is iso-param. Agrees with Looped-DiT (2609.40305) and LM work on extrapolation collapse and the value of deep supervision for robustness across depths.

title: LoopVL: Recurrent Visual Intelligence
relevance_reason: HRM-style nested Module-Loop / Model-Loop recurrent language backbone for a vision-language model trained from scratch, visual tokens updated across loops.
one_sentence: LoopVL-1B nests a low-level module loop (L x3) inside a high-level model loop (x2), executing 128 layer calls from 32 unique layers; at a matched 0.14T-token budget it beats a same-unique-layer 1B Transformer-VL and rivals 4B deep/wide models with less training FLOPs.
key_contributions: Recurrent VLM where visual and text tokens form a unified state updated across nested loops (schedule [L x3 -> H] x2).
Iso-data comparison vs Transformer-VL 1B (same unique layers) and 4B deep/wide baselines at 0.14T tokens.
Ablations: H/L organization matters at equal unrolled depth; extrapolating model cycles beyond training degrades sharply.

setup.model_sizes: ~1B language backbone (32 unique layers, hidden 1536); baselines Transformer-VL 1B and 4B (Deep: 78 layers, Wide: hidden 2816)
setup.train_tokens_or_data: 75B-token text pretraining (incl. 60B HRM-Text base), multimodal training, 16.81B-token SFT, 0.006B-token RL; matched-baseline study at 0.14T tokens
setup.baselines: Transformer-VL 1B/4B (Deep, Wide) at same token budget; public VLMs (InternVL3.5, Qwen3.5, Gemma-4, LFM2-VL)
setup.benchmarks: MMStar, RealWorldQA, ChartQA, AI2D, MathVision, MMMU-Pro, VisuLogic, MMK12, VMCBench

claims.claim: At the same training-token budget and same unique layers, the looped VLM (128 layer calls) beats the 32-layer non-recurrent model on all benchmarks.
claims.regime: iso_param, iso_data (more inference/training FLOPs for LoopVL)
claims.evidence_quote: For example, LoopVL improves MMStar from 55.33 to 63.47, RealWorldQA from 55.29 to 70.98, and ChartQA from 51.12 to 74.52.

claims.claim: At equal unrolled depth, the H/L organization changes results (H2L1 beats H1L3 at 64 calls).
claims.evidence_quote: Notably, H1L3 and H2L1 both execute 64 Transformer-layer calls, yet H2L1 performs better on all five tasks.

claims.claim: Running more model cycles than trained collapses performance (no test-time extrapolation).
claims.evidence_quote: Holding L3 fixed, H3L3 and H4L3 execute 192 and 256 Transformer-layer calls, respectively, compared with 128 under H2L3. Nevertheless, MMStar declines from 63.47 to 58.20 and 24.00, with the same ordering across all five benchmarks.

numbers.what: Training FLOPs of 4B deep/wide baselines vs LoopVL
numbers.quote: FLOPs of the two larger models are 2.89 × 10 and 2.99 × 10 , respectively, compared with 2.47 × 10 for

numbers.what: Text pretraining tokens
numbers.quote: The text pretraining stage uses a total of 75B tokens, including 60B from the HRM-Text base

limitations: No test-time depth extrapolation; early readout gives unparseable outputs; public-model comparisons are unmatched.
survey_notes: Largest multimodal looped model in this group with a clean iso-data/iso-param baseline; reproduces LM findings that trained schedule is optimal and extra loops degrade sharply (contrast Huginn-style randomized-depth training). Supports the 'organization of loops matters at equal unrolled depth' point (also TTS 2609.29768, SPIN 2207.10237).

title: Test-Time Compute Scaling for ASR with Depth-Conditioned Looped Transformers
relevance_reason: Looped shared 4-block ASR encoder with sparse intermediate CTC checkpoints, supervision-clock embeddings, FiLM depth conditioning and delayed soft-posterior feedback.
one_sentence: LARM loops a shared 4-block encoder K=12 times with CTC supervision every c=4 loops, FiLM loop-index conditioning and shifted CTC-posterior feedback; at 7.7M params it beats a 28.9M 16-block unshared encoder on LibriSpeech 100h and WER improves with more test loops.
key_contributions: Encoder-level test-time compute axis for non-autoregressive CTC ASR.
Sparse CTC checkpoints plus periodic clock embeddings and FiLM depth conditioning to specialize shared weights per loop.
Delayed prediction feedback: one-frame-shifted soft CTC posteriors re-injected each loop.

setup.model_sizes: 7.7M (d=384, 4 shared blocks) up to d=1024; baselines 4-block single pass, 16-block unshared (28.9M), 48-block standard
setup.train_tokens_or_data: LibriSpeech train-clean-100 (100h) and train-960
setup.loops_test: up to K at supervised checkpoints
setup.baselines: Same 4-block stack once (iso-param), 16-block unshared, 48-block standard encoder (matched params and block applications at d=1024), naive loop
setup.benchmarks: LibriSpeech test-clean, test-other WER (greedy CTC, 4-gram LM)

claims.claim: LARM beats the parameter-matched single-pass encoder and a 16-block unshared encoder with 3.75x more parameters (LARM uses 48 block passes, so more FLOPs than the 16-block model).
claims.regime: iso_param (vs 4-block once); vs 16-block: fewer params, more FLOPs; iso_data
claims.evidence_quote: On the 100h setting, LARM also outperforms the 16-block unshared encoder while using only 7.7M parameters, compared to 28.9M parameters.

claims.claim: Naive looping already helps over the non-looped encoder, but the loop-structuring mechanisms add further gains.
claims.evidence_quote: Naive recurrence already substantially improves over the non-looped 4-block encoder, see Table 3a, confirming that recurrent depth is useful. However, full LARM further reduces WER from 12.70 to 11.34

claims.claim: Against a 48-block standard encoder matched in parameters and block applications, the largest LARM is only competitive (not better).
claims.evidence_quote: Relative to the 48-block standard encoder, the largest LARM model remains competitive while preserving the shared-parameter recurrent structure.

numbers.what: Best LARM WER (960h, d=1024, greedy)
numbers.quote: Combining larger data with wider encoders further improves performance, reaching 3.39 and 9.01 WER on test-clean and test-other, respectively, for d = 1024.

limitations: Width gains saturate at d=1024; only LibriSpeech; intermediate unsupervised loops can be non-monotonic.
survey_notes: Speech evidence consistent with vision: naive looping helps somewhat but loop-index conditioning plus intermediate supervision are needed. At the cleanest regime (iso-param and iso-block-applications) looping only ties a standard deep encoder, matching the bViT crossroads finding (2608.04879) that looping wins mainly at iso-param, not iso-FLOP.

title: Tiny Recursive Control: Iterative Reasoning for Efficient Optimal Control
relevance_reason: TRM-style two-level recursive network (shared reasoning module applied K x (n+1) times) refining control sequences using simulated trajectory error.
one_sentence: TRC applies a ~1.5M-parameter shared reasoning module through high/low-level latents for K=3 outer iterations (n=4-6 inner cycles), each simulating dynamics and correcting the control from tracking error; it matches SQP optimal cost on Van der Pol and handles powered descent.
key_contributions: Imports TRM's two-level recursion to continuous optimal control; dynamics simulation in the loop provides error feedback.
1.5M parameters, under 10 MB memory, millisecond GPU inference.
Shows >90% cost reduction from iteration 0 to 3 and latent convergence to an attractor.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: Supervised from optimal trajectories: Van der Pol 10,000 train / 1,000 test; powered descent dataset from Briden et al.
setup.loops_train: K = 3 outer, n = 4-6 inner (15-21 module applications)
setup.baselines: Optimal solvers (SQP, successive convexification); language-model baselines (sizes only)
setup.benchmarks: Van der Pol stabilization, powered descent guidance (control cost)

claims.claim: Recursive refinement drives control cost down by over 90% from iteration 0 to 3 on the nonlinear oscillator, reaching the SQP-optimal mean cost.
claims.regime: same model across iterations; vs optimal solver
claims.evidence_quote: The phase portrait demonstrates effective nonlinear control synthesis, with TRC achieving mean control cost of 79.6, matching the optimal cost exactly.

claims.claim: TRC needs far less memory than language-model controllers; comparison is size-only, not matched-task performance.
claims.evidence_quote: TRC achieves near-optimal control costs while requiring only millisecond-scale inference on GPU and under 10 MB memory, two orders of magnitude smaller than language model baselines.

limitations: No stability certificates; requires optimal trajectories for supervised training; fixed-length controls with clipping/penalty constraints.
survey_notes: Science/control transfer of TRM where the loop includes an external simulator (closed-loop error feedback), a design unavailable in language. No non-recursive matched baseline; claims of 'capacity from iteration depth' are not regime-controlled.

title: Sliced Recursive Transformer
relevance_reason: Recursive ViT that loops each block (weight-shared MHSA/FFN) with unshared non-linear projection layers between loops and sliced group self-attention to cut cost.
one_sentence: SReT applies each ViT block twice with shared weights and unshared non-linear projection layers (NLL) between loops, plus sliced group self-attention to reduce FLOPs; naive recursion on DeiT-Tiny gives about +2% top-1 with no extra parameters.
key_contributions: Naive per-block recursion in ViT improves accuracy at constant parameters; NLL between recursions avoids identity-like trivial solutions.
Sliced (group) self-attention across recursive layers cuts 10-30% compute without accuracy loss.
Enables 100-1000 shared-layer ViTs at 13-15M params.

setup.train_tokens_or_data: ImageNet-1K
setup.loops_train: 2 loops per block typical; naive 1x-3x recursion ablation

claims.claim: Plain (naive) recursion improves a ViT by about 2% top-1 at the same parameter count, with extra compute.
claims.evidence_quote: The proposed method can obtain a substantial gain (∼2%) simply using naı̈ve recursive operation, requires no special or sophisticated knowledge for designing principles of networks

claims.claim: More naive recursions stop helping without non-linear projections between loops (cf. Table 1: 1x recursion helps, 3x no further gain).
claims.evidence_quote: As shown in Table 1, more recursions will not improve accuracy without NLL.

claims.claim: Deeper unshared DeiT does not gain, whereas recursive reuse does (deep-supplement ablation).
claims.regime: iso_effective_depth (deeper DeiT vs recursive), more params for DeiT
claims.evidence_quote: We can see deeper naı̈ve DeiT could not bring additional gain on performance since the deeper and heavier network is usually more difficult to learn meaningful and diverse intermediate features

numbers.what: SReT-ExT vs DeiT-T
numbers.quote: SReT-ExT FLOPs: 0.7B↓46.2% #Params: 4.0M↓29.8% Acc.: 74.0%↑1.8% Throughput: 3473.43 img/s

limitations: Recursion adds compute (mitigated by sliced attention); gains from naive recursion saturate quickly.
survey_notes: Early vision looping paper (2021). Inserting small unshared projections between loops (NLL) is a relaxed-sharing design analogous to step-specific adapters/LoRA in LMs (Relaxed Recursive Transformers). Agrees with SoftMoR (2607.00774) and LARM (2606.04678) that naive looping saturates fast in non-language domains.

title: MergeOver: Post-Training Token Merging for Recursive Vision Transformers
relevance_reason: Post-training token merging for the weight-shared recursive SReT ViT; a systems add-on to a looped vision model, not a new looping method.
one_sentence: MergeOver integrates ToMe token merging into the recursive SReT ViT without retraining (merge once at each stage's first block, keep length fixed through recursions), trading 1.47 pp top-1 for ~37% lower activation memory.
